name: Mahalakshmi Temple, Kolhapur (Ambabai)
deity: Goddess Mahalakshmi, known as Ambabai (Karaveera Mahalakshmi), with Bhairava Krodhisha
period: Ancient Shakta seat, traditionally dated to the Chalukya era (7th century CE); stone temple of the Hemadpanti manner with later restorations
dynasty: Chalukya (traditionally King Karnadeva), with later Maratha-era restoration
summary: The Mahalakshmi temple of Kolhapur, the Karaveera of the old texts, is the great living seat of Ambabai, named in the Ashtadasha Shakti Peetha Stotram and honoured as the place where the eyes of Sati are said to have fallen.

sections.history: Kolhapur, the Karaveera or Karavira of the Puranic tradition, has been a seat of the Goddess for well over a thousand years. Tradition credits the temple to the Chalukya king Karnadeva in about the seventh century; sources differ on the details, the stone shrine seen today is generally placed somewhat later, and worship is recorded as restored in the eighteenth century under the Marathas, whose royal house of Kolhapur long remained her patron. In the Shakta tradition the city is one of the Ashtadasha Maha Shakti Peethas, the eighteen great seats praised in the Ashtadasha Shakti Peetha Stotram attributed to Adi Shankaracharya, which sings of her as Kolhapure Mahalakshmi. It is also counted among the three and a half Shakti Peethas of Maharashtra. Tradition holds that the eyes of Sati fell here, and names the guardian Bhairava as Krodhisha.
sections.architecture: The temple is raised in dark stone in the Hemadpanti manner, close to the heart of the old city on Mahadwar Road. The goddess is enshrined as a self-manifested image of black stone, about three feet tall and crowned, in a small inner sanctum. Three sanctums stand within the complex, their shikharas of brick and mortar rebuilt in the nineteenth century. Facing the main sanctum is a stone mandapa on a raised platform that holds Ganesha, and a later Garuda mandapa of the eighteenth or nineteenth century stands in the courtyard. The sanctum is so aligned that, twice a year, the rays of the setting sun enter it and fall upon the goddess.
sections.legends: The Karveer Mahatmya, a later text told through the voice of the sage Agastya, recounts how the Goddess, as Mahalakshmi, fought the demon Kolhasura, who had tormented the gods. When he fell, it is said, his last wish was that the place should carry his name, and so the city became Kolhapur; in another telling he asked that she remain here and guard it. A popular story adds that after the sage Bhrigu's affront to Vishnu, Lakshmi left Vaikuntha in sorrow and made her home at Kolhapur, though this tale is not found in the older texts. Behind all of these stands the Shakti Peetha story: when Sati gave up her life at her father Daksha's sacrifice, a grief-stricken Shiva carried her body across the land, and wherever its parts fell a seat of the Goddess arose. At Karaveera her eyes are said to have fallen, and the Mother is held to watch over every pilgrim with unending compassion.
sections.festivals: Sharadiya Navaratri, from Ashwin Shuddha Pratipada to Khandenavami, is the greatest festival. The goddess's festival image is carried in a palanquin procession around the temple at night, on Lalita Panchami she visits the Tryambuli temple on the outskirts of the town, and on Vijayadashami her palanquin goes, under the patronage of the Karveer royal house, to Dasara Chowk and on to the Panchaganga river. In Chaitra she is taken around the city in a silver chariot at the Rathotsav. Kiranotsav is the temple's own marvel: twice a year, around 31 January to 2 February and 9 to 11 November, the rays of the setting sun enter the sanctum, touch the goddess's feet, and over the following days rise higher upon her. Dates vary between sources, so confirm them locally.
sections.experience: Come early if you can. The way to the goddess leads through the busy lanes of the old city, past stalls of flowers, coconuts and sweets, into a courtyard where a stream of devotees from across the Deccan moves slowly towards the sanctum. The darshan itself is brief but long remembered: the dark, crowned image in the lamplight, and the calm of a Mother whom the people of Kolhapur simply call Ambabai. Many linger afterwards by the mandapa of Ganesha and in the quieter corners of the courtyard. The evening aarti is especially moving, while Fridays, Navaratri and other festival days bring very large crowds.

visit.timings: Typically open from early morning, around 4:30 AM, until late evening, around 10 PM, with darshan paused briefly for rituals; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left outside the temple.
visit.photography: Photography is generally restricted inside the inner sanctum. Follow the notices displayed at the entrance and ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: The temple stands on Mahadwar Road in the old city of Kolhapur, a short auto-rickshaw or taxi ride from Kolhapur railway station (about 3 to 5 km, sources differ). Kolhapur Airport is roughly 9 to 10 km away. Pune is about 240 km and Mumbai about 380 km by road, with frequent state and private buses to Kolhapur.
